title: Research Bite #55: Fifty Years of A-Level Mathematics: Have Standards Changed?
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #55 covers Ian Jones, Chris Wheadon, Sara Humphries, and Matthew Inglis's 'Fifty-year of A-level mathematics: have standards changed?', published in the British Educational Research Journal (2016), funded by AQA. The researchers used comparative judgement -- having expert judges directly compare pairs of exam scripts rather than mark them independently against a rubric -- to evaluate 66 A-level mathematics scripts spanning from the mid-1960s to 2012. Twenty mathematics PhD students from Loughborough University, recruited specifically because they were unfamiliar with A-level papers and therefore unbiased, judged re-typeset scripts (to remove handwriting and paper-quality cues) and were required to pass a subject-knowledge test to qualify as judges. The headline finding directly challenges a common public narrative: standards did decline meaningfully between the 1960s and the 1990s, but the judges found no evidence of any further decline since the mid-1990s. Barton's summary frames this as good news for teachers currently working under the assumption that rigour keeps eroding -- the data instead shows roughly three decades of stability.
points: The comparative-judgement method itself is a high-impact idea independent of the maths finding: having unbiased expert judges directly compare scripts sidesteps the drift and inconsistency problems of rubric-based marking across different eras.

The finding that standards fell in the 1960s-1990s but have been stable since 1996 directly contradicts the popular 'exams just keep getting easier' narrative, giving teachers a citable counter to that claim.

Using unfamiliar PhD mathematicians as judges (rather than experienced examiners) was a deliberate design choice to remove bias from familiarity with current grading norms -- a methodological detail that strengthens confidence in the result.

Because the study stops at 2012, it cannot speak to standards in the post-2012 reformed A-level curriculum; teachers should treat the 'stability' finding as bounded by that endpoint, not as an open-ended guarantee.

The re-typesetting of scripts to strip handwriting and paper-quality cues before judging is a small methodological detail that meaningfully reduces a specific, easy-to-overlook source of bias in cross-era comparisons.
quotes: Research using comparative judgement indicates that A-level mathematics standards declined significantly between the 1960s and 1990s.
However, experts found no evidence of further decline since the mid-1990s, contradicting popular claims that academic rigour continues to fall.

While A-level mathematics standards declined between the 1960s and 1990s, there is no evidence of a further drop since 1996. Contrary to popular belief, standards have actually remained stable over the last two decades.
Comparative judgement: Experts compare script pairs to identify the better one. Cross-moderation: Examiners review scripts from different exams to judge standards.
Common test: Comparing results from an unchanging test across cohorts. Parameter estimate: A statistical measure of a script's underlying quality derived from repeated pairwise comparisons.
